questions.q: What should be the highest-priority question a reviewer asks on a research team's pull request?
options: Does the variable naming follow the team's style guide?
Does this code actually implement what it claims to implement, correctly matching the paper or spec?
Is the PR description under 100 words?
Does the author have commit access to the main branch?
questions.explain: The highest-value review question is correctness of the experiment — whether the code actually implements the claimed behavior, such as a learning-rate schedule matching its formula and being wired in correctly. Style is a lower-priority, non-blocking concern.

questions.q: Why does fast review turnaround matter more on a research team than on many production teams?
options: Research teams never have urgent deadlines
A PR sitting in review is often a training run sitting idle on expensive, shared compute that other experiments are blocked behind
Research code never needs review at all
Production teams do not use pull requests
questions.explain: On a research team, review delay often directly translates into idle, expensive shared GPU time and blocked downstream experiments, making prompt (even if brief) review far more valuable than on most production teams.

questions.q: What does 'partial unblocking' mean in the context of research code review?
options: Approving a PR without reading it
Approving the sound majority of a diff while flagging a smaller remaining concern as a fast follow-up, rather than blocking the entire PR
Rejecting a PR outright and asking for a full rewrite
Giving every PR the same fixed review time regardless of size
questions.explain: Rather than blocking an entire PR over one small issue, a reviewer can approve the sound majority of the change and flag the remaining concern as a quick follow-up, keeping the team's iteration speed high.

questions.q: Why does a config diff like changing a learning rate from 0.1 to 1.0 deserve the same review scrutiny as a code change?
options: Config files are technically written in Python
A small config change can silently and significantly alter experiment behavior, just as consequentially as a large code refactor, and is easy to wave through as 'just a config file'
YAML files cannot be reviewed in most tools
Config diffs are always wrong by default
questions.explain: A one-line hyperparameter change can be far more consequential to an experiment's outcome than a large code refactor, yet it's easy to approve without scrutiny simply because it isn't traditional source code.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should review intensity relate to a change's 'blast radius'?
options: All changes should receive identical, maximum scrutiny regardless of scope
Review intensity should scale with blast radius — heavier scrutiny for shared infrastructure like the training loop, lighter for a one-off experiment script
Only changes made by junior engineers need review
Blast radius is irrelevant to how a change should be reviewed
questions.explain: Changes to shared infrastructure that many experiments depend on warrant heavier review, while low-stakes, easily-reverted changes affecting a single experiment can reasonably receive lighter scrutiny and faster turnaround.
